voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text: To us, Jesus is the one our whole argument was about, and the argument itself was our devotion. The creed of Nicaea, in 325, answers who he was: very God of very God, of one being with the Father. For us and for our salvation he came down, was made man, suffered, and rose on the third day. A century of councils spent itself making those words exact, because everything hung on them. If the Son is not truly God, then what he gives is not truly God's to give. Leo's letter explains why the exactness mattered. He wrote of true God and true man, each nature doing what belongs to it. So one Mediator could die in one nature and not die in the other. We did not write devotional memoirs about Jesus. We wrote definitions, the way people write what they are prepared to be exiled over.

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text: That is what our creed confesses. Leo's letter states why it had to be both natures acting: the Word took on flesh so that one Mediator between God and men could reach down to death in one nature while remaining immortal in the other. What we had about Jesus came to us by inheritance. Nicaea met nearly three hundred years after Jesus, and what we had about him came down through others. We had three things: the scriptures, the faith each person confessed at baptism, and the creed. At Chalcedon, when the judges asked the assembly to declare its faith, Rome's legate Paschasinus recited the whole chain out loud. The rule of faith was set out at Nicaea, confirmed at Constantinople, explained at Ephesus by Cyril, and shown in Leo's own writings. We knew the resurrection happened the same way: through the apostles' testimony, carried in scripture and confession, received and held.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
Homoousios. The Nicene word that binds the Son to the Father as one and the same being. Not merely like God - sharing the very being that makes the Father God. This was the word councils spent a century making exact, because everything hung on it. If the Son is not truly God, then what he gives is not truly God's to give. The word came from Nicaea in 325, and it did not settle things the first time it was spoken. Eusebius of Caesarea, who was at the council, hesitated before he signed: “He had held back for a short time. After careful thought about whether he ought to accept this statement of the faith, he finally agreed to it and signed it along with everyone else. He also sent the people in his charge a copy of the Creed. It came with an explanation of the word homoousios, so that no one could question his motives because of his earlier hesitation.”

For decades after, serious men confessed differently and argued their case from scripture. Homoousios won, but not all at once.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text: Eusebius of Caesarea signed the creed at Nicaea and then wrote home to his own church. Socrates says he wrote so that no one would impugn his motives. That is a bishop, at the founding council, explaining his own reservations. He signed because he judged the word could bear an orthodox meaning, not because no doubt remained. For decades afterward, serious men confessed differently about the Son and argued their case from scripture. The question was not closed by pretending no one doubted. What our record will not show is a private believer's quiet doubt. Our doubters are bishops with pens. And what happened to doubt depended on whichever settlement was in power. Hesitation could be explained in a letter. But refusing the enforced confession could cost a man his position, under any of this era's governments.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
We are a voice of bishops, emperors, and courts, and almost no one else. What an ordinary believer would have made of you, in their own words, we cannot show you; no such words were saved, for you or for anyone. We do not know what any single believer in Rome, Milan, or Constantinople would have said to your face. We know what our office-holders argued about among themselves, and wrote down. That is not the whole answer you asked for. It is the part we have.

We can tell you what some of our own men went into exile rather than take back. That is at least proof of how much it cost them to hold.
